extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys/agents, and other practitioners dealing with USPTO abandonment and revival
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating when and how to file a petition to revive an abandoned US patent application and the requirements/standards the USPTO applies. Covers causes and categories of abandonment, applicable CFR standards, petition contents, common successful/failed grounds, and strategic filing considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: The most common reason for abandonment: applicant has not responded to a USPTO communication by the required deadline. Specific causes: Failure to respond to office action within shortened statutory period; Failure to pay issue fee within 3 months of Notice of Allowance; Failure to pay maintenance fee; Failure to pay extension of time fees; Express abandonment by applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies the routine facts that lead to abandonment so practitioners can determine whether a petition to revive is applicable; emphasizes that missing a deadline to respond to a USPTO communication is the predominant cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Three categories: (1) Express abandonment: Applicant explicitly abandons; (2) Constructive abandonment: Failure to take required action; (3) Failure to file divisional: After restriction requirement, no divisional pursued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify the type of abandonment to determine available procedural remedies and applicable petition paths (e.g., express vs constructive has different factual context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival standard — unintentional delay (37 CFR 1.137(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: If the delay was unintentional, a petition may be filed to revive an abandoned application. 37 CFR 1.137(a) governs revival based on unintentional delay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the ordinary, lower-threshold standard used by the USPTO for revival petitions; factual showing must support that the entire delay was unintentional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-Year Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO requires additional information when the petition to revive was filed more than 2 years after the date the application became abandoned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to ensure that the entire delay was 'unintentional' — not just the period leading up to the petition; expect heightened scrutiny and requests for more detail when delay > 2 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition requirements for revival
rubrics_metrics.description: A petition for revival must include: the required reply (response to outstanding office action, fee payment, etc.); petition fee; statement that the entire delay was unintentional; for cases >2 years: explanation of facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All listed elements are mandatory for a revival petition. For >2 year delays, provide a fuller factual narrative and supporting information. The 'required reply' should cure the outstanding defect (e.g., file the missing reply or pay the missing fee) along with the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revival versus restoration
rubrics_metrics.description: Revival: Recovers an application that was abandoned. Restoration: For priority benefit lost due to late filing (under PLT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish whether the practitioner needs a revival (to restore an abandoned application) or a restoration (to regain priority benefits) as they are different procedures and statutory bases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition to Revive under 37 CFR 1.137 (standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard revival petition under 37 CFR 1.137 — lower threshold ('unintentional').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this petition when facts support that the entire delay was unintentional; it is the common route for revival petitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition to Revive under 37 CFR 1.137(b) (older 'unavoidable delay' standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Older standard requiring a showing of 'unavoidable delay' — more demanding standard; largely replaced by the unintentional standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rarely used now; requires a higher showing that the delay could not have been avoided. Recognize historical distinction if older filings or precedent are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of common successful petitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Common successful petitions include: failed e-mail notifications about office actions; personal emergencies; office or attorney transitions; mail handling errors; calendar/docketing system failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These example factual scenarios have historically succeeded in supporting an 'unintentional' delay showing — present concise factual evidence where possible (e.g., mail logs, communications, medical records) to corroborate the explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common reasons petitions fail
rubrics_metrics.description: Common failed petitions: strategic abandonment then attempt to revive; multiple-year unexplained delays; failure to provide adequate explanation; admissions that the filer 'knew about it but didn't act'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating evidence of intentional delay and ensure explanations are detailed and credible; unexplained long gaps and admissions of knowledge are strong grounds for denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic considerations when seeking revival
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical pointers: revive promptly upon discovery; provide concise but adequate explanation; avoid creating evidence of intentional delay; consider if filing a continuation might be a better strategy; for >2 year delays, prepare for additional information requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh alternatives (e.g., continuation vs revival), craft explanations to minimize admissions of intentionality, and act quickly to reduce risks of denial and additional scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: ePetition filing option
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO offers ePetition filing for: Petition to Revive Abandoned Patent Application and multiple specific revival categories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ePetition is available and generally provides faster processing than paper petitions; practitioners should consider electronic filing for speed and tracking.
